Water hyacinth biochar was produced by pyrolysis at 400, 500, and 600°C under nitrogen gas flow.
WHBC-PVA composites were fabricated by blending 16 g biochar with 100 cm3 of 1% w/v PVA solution.
Composite disks were 0.5 cm thick and 9.5 cm in diameter for sound absorption testing.
Surface area of WHBC600-PVA composite was highest at 27,378 m2/g with pore volume of 0.045 cm3/g.
Sound absorption coefficient (SAC) of WHBC-PVA ranged from 0.0650 to 0.2103, outperforming Styrofoam's SAC of 0.0437.
The impedance tube used for testing was 95 cm long with 9.5 cm inner diameter.
Sound frequency for absorption testing was 440 Hz at 84 dB sound intensity.
FTIR spectra showed O-H, C=O, C=C, and aromatic functional groups in the composite.
SEM analysis revealed irregular surface morphology without regular patterns.
Nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms indicated H3 type hysteresis loops, typical of slit-shaped mesopores.
Porosity was calculated based on volume of voids divided by total volume of the composite disk.
Water hyacinth grows rapidly, doubling in 5-15 days under optimal conditions.
Biochar production increased pH to alkaline range (~8.11) compared to raw water hyacinth (~6.1).
Nitrogen condensation in pores during BET analysis indicated cylindrical mesopores of 2-50 nm size.
The composite's sound absorption is especially effective at low frequency around 440 Hz.
WHBC-PVA composite formation involves hydrogen bonding between C=O groups of biochar and O-H groups of PVA.
The study used a Bluetooth speaker and sound meter software for wireless sound transmission and recording.
The composite showed better sound absorption than original water hyacinth powder mixed with wood glue or PVC adhesives.
The porous structure includes interparticle voids (macropores) and intraparticle mesopores enhancing sound absorption.
The composite fabrication involved drying at 110°C for 24 hours to form solid disks.
